Romans 1: Paul writes from Corinth about AD 57, near the end of his third journey, to a church in Rome he has not yet visited (Romans 1:10–13). Nero had been emperor since AD 54.
Romans 2: Paul argues as if with a questioner. Rome's Jews had been expelled by Claudius about AD 49 (Acts 18:2) and returned after his death in AD 54.
Romans 3: Paul quotes a chain of Psalms and Isaiah to show that both Jews and Gentiles are under sin.
Romans 4: Paul uses Abraham, counted righteous before he was circumcised (Genesis 15:6; 17:24), as his example.
Romans 5: Paul compares Adam, through whom sin entered the world, with Christ.
Romans 6: Paul writes to believers who had been baptized and to a city where slaves made up a large share of the population.
Romans 7: Paul speaks "to them that know the law" (Romans 7:1).
Romans 8: Paul writes of life in the Spirit and of suffering "for thy sake we are killed all the day long" (Romans 8:36), quoting Psalm 44:22.
Romans 9: Paul begins three chapters (Romans 9–11) on Israel, grieving that many of his own people have not believed (Romans 9:1–3; 10:1).
Romans 10: Paul continues on Israel, quoting Deuteronomy, Isaiah, and Joel.
Romans 11: Paul addresses Gentile believers directly and compares them to wild olive branches grafted in.
Romans 12: Paul turns to practical instruction for life together in the church.
Romans 13: Paul writes about governing authorities and taxes to believers in the capital, early in Nero's reign, before the persecution of AD 64.
Romans 14: Paul addresses disputes over food and holy days among Jewish and Gentile believers.
Romans 15: Paul is about to take a collection from Macedonia and Achaia to Jerusalem, then hopes to visit Rome on the way to Spain (Romans 15:24–26).
Romans 16: Paul commends Phebe of Cenchrea, Corinth's eastern port, and greets about twenty-six people in Rome, including Priscilla and Aquila, back from Corinth and Ephesus.
1 Corinthians 1: Paul writes from Ephesus about AD 54–55 (1 Corinthians 16:8) to the church he founded in Corinth about AD 50–51 (Acts 18). Members of Chloe's household have reported divisions.
1 Corinthians 2: Paul recalls coming to Corinth "in weakness, and in fear" (1 Corinthians 2:3) after his visit to Athens (Acts 17–18).
1 Corinthians 3: Paul addresses rivalry over himself and Apollos, who had taught in Corinth after him (Acts 18:27–19:1).
1 Corinthians 4: Paul says he is sending Timothy to Corinth (1 Corinthians 4:17).
1 Corinthians 5: Paul mentions an earlier letter he had written to them (1 Corinthians 5:9), which has not survived.
1 Corinthians 6: Paul addresses believers taking each other to court before Roman judges.
1 Corinthians 7: Paul begins answering a letter the Corinthians wrote to him (1 Corinthians 7:1).
1 Corinthians 8: Paul answers their question about meat offered to idols, common in Corinth's temples and market.
1 Corinthians 9: Paul defends his practice of working rather than taking support. Corinth hosted the Isthmian Games every two years.
1 Corinthians 10: Paul recalls Israel in the wilderness and returns to the question of idol meat sold in the shambles (meat market).
1 Corinthians 11: Paul addresses head coverings and the Lord's supper, which was eaten as part of a shared meal in homes.
1 Corinthians 12: Paul begins three chapters (1 Corinthians 12–14) on spiritual gifts.
1 Corinthians 13: Paul's chapter on love sits between his teaching on spiritual gifts.
1 Corinthians 14: Paul gives order for tongues and prophecy in the gathered church.
1 Corinthians 15: Some in Corinth deny the resurrection. Paul lists appearances of the risen Jesus, including to more than five hundred at once, "of whom the greater part remain" (1 Corinthians 15:6).
1 Corinthians 16: Paul plans to stay at Ephesus until Pentecost (1 Corinthians 16:8) and gives instructions for the Jerusalem collection.
2 Corinthians 1: Paul writes from Macedonia about AD 55–56, after trouble in Asia (2 Corinthians 1:8) and a change of travel plans.
2 Corinthians 2: Paul mentions a painful visit and a letter written "with many tears" (2 Corinthians 2:4), and his search for Titus at Troas.
2 Corinthians 3: Paul defends his ministry to readers who expect letters of commendation.
2 Corinthians 4: Paul writes of being "troubled on every side" (2 Corinthians 4:8) in his travels.
2 Corinthians 5: Paul writes of the earthly body as a tent and of the judgment seat of Christ.
2 Corinthians 6: Paul lists hardships of his ministry, including imprisonments and riots (2 Corinthians 6:5).
2 Corinthians 7: Titus has met Paul in Macedonia with good news from Corinth (2 Corinthians 7:5–7).
2 Corinthians 8: Paul urges Corinth to complete the collection for Jerusalem, as the churches of Macedonia have done.
2 Corinthians 9: Paul is sending brothers ahead so the Corinthian gift will be ready when he arrives with Macedonians.
2 Corinthians 10: Paul answers critics in Corinth who say his letters are weighty but his presence weak.
2 Corinthians 11: Paul lists his sufferings, including escaping from Damascus under King Aretas (2 Corinthians 11:32–33), Nabataean king until about AD 40.
2 Corinthians 12: Paul tells of a vision "above fourteen years ago" (2 Corinthians 12:2), in the early 40s AD, and plans a third visit.
2 Corinthians 13: Paul warns that his third visit is coming. Acts 20:2–3 records three months in Greece soon after.
Galatians 1: Paul writes to churches in Galatia, in central Asia Minor, probably about AD 48–55. He recounts his conversion, three years in Arabia and Damascus, and a fifteen-day visit to Peter in Jerusalem (Galatians 1:17–18).
Galatians 2: Fourteen years later Paul goes to Jerusalem with Barnabas and Titus (Galatians 2:1), then confronts Peter at Antioch.
Galatians 3: Teachers have urged the Galatian believers, mostly Gentiles, to be circumcised and keep the law.
Galatians 4: Paul recalls first preaching in Galatia "through infirmity of the flesh" (Galatians 4:13).
Galatians 5: Paul warns the Galatians not to accept circumcision as a requirement.
Galatians 6: Paul closes the letter in his own large handwriting (Galatians 6:11).
Ephesians 1: The letter names Paul, a prisoner, as its author and Ephesus as its destination, though some early manuscripts omit "at Ephesus" (Ephesians 1:1). Many date it to Paul's Roman imprisonment, about AD 60–62; some scholars think a later follower wrote it.
Ephesians 2: The letter reminds Gentile readers that they were once "far off" and speaks of the wall between Jew and Gentile, like the barrier in the Jerusalem temple courts.
Ephesians 3: Paul writes as "the prisoner of Jesus Christ for you Gentiles" (Ephesians 3:1).
Ephesians 4: The letter urges unity and "walk worthy" from Paul "the prisoner of the Lord" (Ephesians 4:1).
Ephesians 5: Instructions for households begin, addressed to wives and husbands.
Ephesians 6: The household instructions continue with children, servants, and masters. Tychicus carries the letter (Ephesians 6:21).
Philippians 1: Paul writes from prison, probably in Rome about AD 60–62, though Ephesus and Caesarea have also been proposed, to the church he founded at Philippi about AD 50 (Acts 16).
Philippians 2: Paul plans to send Timothy and is sending back Epaphroditus, who nearly died while visiting him (Philippians 2:25–30).
Philippians 3: Paul warns against those who insist on circumcision and lists his own Jewish credentials.
Philippians 4: Paul thanks the Philippians for gifts sent with Epaphroditus and sends greetings from "Caesar's household" (Philippians 4:22).
Colossians 1: The letter is from Paul and Timothy to Colossae in the Lycus valley, a church founded by Epaphras (Colossians 1:7). It is usually dated to Paul's Roman imprisonment, about AD 60–62.
Colossians 2: Paul has not met the believers at Colossae or Laodicea (Colossians 2:1). He warns against teachings about food, festivals, and angels.
Colossians 3: Instructions for households, similar to Ephesians 5–6, are addressed to wives, husbands, children, fathers, servants, and masters.
Colossians 4: Tychicus and Onesimus carry the letter (Colossians 4:7–9), probably together with the letter to Philemon. An earthquake struck Laodicea about AD 60 (Tacitus).
